Пожар в Юганском заповеднике, 27.07.2012

A big patch of mostly coniferous forest burning in the Yuganskiy nature reserve. The tiny pale-green spot on the right is a small peatbog where the helicopter dropped us off. A day later the fire approached the bog, turning our little mycological journey into something a bit too extreme :)

images.caption:
Сибиа Ан-2  / Sibia An-2 RA-54946
An Antonov An-2 flying over us, inspecting the extent of the progressing fire. 
An-2 is an old and reliable workhorse of the Russian civil aviation - it made its maiden flight in 1947. 

When it flew over us, there was a strange feeling of traveling back in time - pristine taiga, absolutely no one around, navigating with a map and compass - and being on a romantic, patriotic, and at the same time unreasonably unsafe and basically useless mission. It felt very... Soviet :)))

images.caption:
Пожар в Юганском заповеднике, 27.07.2012
We'd been planning this trip for a while. My mycologist friend invited me to visit her in her home village and go look for mushrooms together (officially - as part of the monitoring fieldwork for the publication of the 2013 Red List of Yugra). The initial plan was to take a boat (or, we were lucky, a helicopter) to one of the remote field bases in the reserve and collect specimens there - Yugra also suffered from drought this year, but not as severely as Novosibirsk and other more southern regions, so there was some hope we could find at least some fungi.
A few days before my flight to Surgut (a transitional point on the way to Ugut, which is a few hundred km to the South up the river Yugan) Lena called and said that we wouldn't be able to go to the nature reserve, because there were big forest fires everywhere and emergency situation had been declared, cancelling all local flights and banning civilians from visiting forests....
Nevertheless...
I'd packed all my stuff and was ready to go to the airport here in Novosibirsk, Lena called and told me not to go far from the Surgut airport when I get there - a helicopter taking firefighters to a big forest fire was supposed to fly from Surgut through Ugut and it could pick me up, too. That's what I understood. 
I didn't realize I'd be the only passenger on that Mi-8, and that 6 guys that waited on the helicopter pad in Ugut and joined me in the chopper were not firefighters at all, but regular park employees (including Lena!). They'd been equipped with high-tech firefighting gadgets (a bunch of shovels, two spraying backpacks  and a chainsaw)  and sent by their boss to stop a big fire in the square 510 of the nature reserve. Neither did I (or any of the 7 of us) realize that the chopper would simply drop us off (all of us - including us girls) directly near the fire and leave us there for good with a non-functional radio and a satellite phone with half-dead batteries.

In the end, everything was fine - pure luck! - but it was a hell of a week. The company was very nice, though, and we even managed to find some fungi :)

images.caption:
Пожар в Юганском заповеднике, 27.07.2012

Everything seemed rather peaceful on the first day - they guys went to check the extent of the fire, which then seemed to be somewhere rather far away - we couldn't feel its presence except maybe for the constant "bonfire" smell in the air and pale sky (but it was not surprising at all, there has been a lot of smog all over Siberia throughout this summer); Lena and I went to have a look around the place, following a dried-out creek, and try to find some fungi - which we actually did.

I took this picture in the evening - you can see that the air got "whiter" compared to the pictures below....

images.caption:
This Helix Mi-8 took me from Surgut to Ugut, and then from Ugut to the southwesternmost corner of the Yuganskiy nature reserve.


I spent two weeks in a small log cabin in taiga with the two guys in camo suits - we went grouse counting and mushroom hunting (not vice versa, honestly) :) It was absolutely awesome.

images.caption:
this species is very common in late summer in dry pine forests around Ugut. Smaller clusters can be confused with another Lyophyllum species that was formerly thought to be L. fumosum - but now specialists say it's the valuable L. shimeji. It's a misunderstood group of species and only recently taxonomic research by a group of Swedish mycologists supported by molecular studies made the picture clearer. 

anyway, this species is edible and very tasty!
